title: 2 Kings 23:1–14
context: Josiah reads the book of the covenant to all the people, renews the covenant, and purges Judah’s worship: removing vessels and priests of Baal and the army of the sky, defiling the high places, ending the child sacrifice at Topheth, and tearing down altars built by Ahaz, Manasseh, and Solomon.

verses.text: The king sent, and they gathered to him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The king gathers all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. Arminian readers see Josiah drawing the nation’s leaders into his response to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king leading the people toward covenant renewal. The gathering marks the transition from private conviction to public action.

verses.text: The king went up to the LORD’s house, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him—with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, both small and great; and he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The king reads “all the words of the book of the covenant” before the people, “both small and great.” Arminian readers see God’s word made available to everyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the public reading as central to reform. Readers in both traditions commonly regard this scene as shared ground on the renewing power of God’s word.

verses.text: The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes with all his heart and all his soul, to confirm the words of this covenant that were written in this book; and all the people agreed to the covenant.
verses.arminianNotes: The king makes a covenant “to walk after the LORD,” and “all the people agreed to the covenant.” Arminian readers see a sincere commitment freely made by king and people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant renewal in response to God’s word. The phrase “with all his heart and all his soul” echoes Deuteronomy’s call to wholehearted love.

verses.text: The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the threshold, to bring out of the LORD’s temple all the vessels that were made for Baal, for the Asherah, and for all the army of the sky; and he burned them outside of Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron, and carried their ashes to Bethel.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah orders the removal and burning of vessels made for Baal, Asherah, and the army of the sky. Arminian readers see decisive action following the covenant commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cleansing of the temple. The ashes carried to Bethel anticipate Josiah’s later actions there in verses 15–20.

verses.text: He got rid of the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah and in the places around Jerusalem; those also who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, to the moon, to the planets, and to all the army of the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: He removes the idolatrous priests who burned incense to Baal, the sun, moon, planets, and the army of the sky. Arminian readers see reform reaching the leaders of false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a thorough reform of Judah’s worship. The list shows how widespread idolatry had become under previous kings.

verses.text: He brought out the Asherah from the LORD’s house, outside of Jerusalem, to the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and beat it to dust, and cast its dust on the graves of the common people.
verses.arminianNotes: He burns the Asherah at the brook Kidron, beats it to dust, and casts the dust on common graves. Arminian readers see the complete destruction of an object of idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the desecration of the idol. The account records the actions without elaboration, keeping the focus on the removal of false worship.

verses.text: He broke down the houses of the male shrine prostitutes that were in the LORD’s house, where the women wove hangings for the Asherah.
verses.arminianNotes: He breaks down the houses of the male shrine prostitutes in the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see the removal of practices that defiled God’s sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cleansing of the temple from cultic immorality. The narrator states the facts plainly and without sensational detail.

verses.text: He brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba; and he broke down the high places of the gates that were at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which were on a man’s left hand at the gate of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: He brings the priests from Judah’s cities and defiles the high places “from Geba to Beersheba.” Arminian readers see reform extending throughout the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the centralization of worship according to the law. The phrase “from Geba to Beersheba” indicates the full extent of Judah’s territory.

verses.text: Nevertheless the priests of the high places didn’t come up to the LORD’s altar in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their brothers.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests of the high places do not come to the LORD’s altar but eat unleavened bread with their brothers. Arminian readers see a measured response that limits their role without abandoning them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a careful distinction in their treatment. The verse shows reform that addressed false worship while still providing for these priests.

verses.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
verses.arminianNotes: “He defiled Topheth … that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.” Arminian readers grieve the child sacrifice once practiced there and see Josiah ending it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise name the practice soberly and see the reform protecting children from idolatrous sacrifice. Jeremiah 7:31 also condemns what was done at Topheth.

verses.text: He took away the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, at the entrance of the LORD’s house, by the room of Nathan Melech the officer who was in the court; and he burned the chariots of the sun with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: He removes the horses dedicated to the sun and burns the chariots of the sun. Arminian readers see the removal of objects tied to sun worship at the temple entrance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the purging of solar worship. Readers in this tradition generally hedge comparisons with ancient Near Eastern sun cults, since the text gives few details.

verses.text: The king broke down the altars that were on the roof of the upper room of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the LORD’s house, and beat them down from there, and cast their dust into the brook Kidron.
verses.arminianNotes: He breaks down the altars on the roof of Ahaz’s upper room and the altars Manasseh made in the temple courts. Arminian readers see Josiah undoing the idolatry of previous kings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see reform reversing the corruption introduced by Ahaz and Manasseh. The verse links back to 21:5, showing Manasseh’s altars removed.

verses.text: The king defiled the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mountain of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: He defiles the high places Solomon built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. Arminian readers see reform reaching back to idolatry introduced by Solomon himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah addressing long-standing apostasy recorded in 1 Kings 11:7. The phrase “mountain of corruption” is the narrator’s description, and its exact location is debated.

verses.text: He broke in pieces the pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their places with men’s bones.
verses.arminianNotes: He breaks the pillars, cuts down the Asherah poles, and fills their places with human bones. Arminian readers see the final defilement of idolatrous sites to prevent their reuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a thorough end to these places of false worship. The catalog of reforms closes here, recorded soberly and without embellishment.
